speakeroldname: Righi Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a further statement with respect to the Middle East situation, particularly in connection with the United Nations security council and the discussions which are taking place there at this time.
Yesterday I was not in a position to reveal to the house the manner in which it was proposed to arrange a meeting at the heads of government level while preserving the primary responsibility of the United Nations security council. Everything that has been done in the last two or three days-and I am not restricting my remarks to that period-[DOT] has been designed to ensure that this matter shall be considered by the United Nations and that action outside of the United Nations shall not be taken.
Hon. members will have learned that Mr. Selwyn Lloyd, United Kingdom foreign secretary, announced in the House of Commons at Westminster this morning that if an extraordinary special session of the security council were convened in order to discuss Middle East questions, Prime Minister Macmillan would be willing to attend if other heads of government concerned were prepared to do likewise. As Mr. Lloyd pointed out, certain questions concerning the Middle East are already under consideration in the security council and it is only appropriate that the higher level talks now envisaged should take place in the same forum to provide for continuity.
The basis for such a meeting would, however, differ from the normal proceedings in the security council in that it would proceed by consultation rather than by resolution and would attempt to formulate binding conclusions only on the basis of mutual agreement. This would provide a flexible procedure which
would permit the consultation at heads of government level to be a continuous process in which countries not members of the security council could be invited to participate as might be appropriate. Such a special meeting could meet publicly or in restricted session. It could make its own arrangements for future meetings and would adhere to no fixed timetable or agenda.
The initiative that has been taken is, I think, the kind of novel and I trust effective proposal which the present grave situation requires, and I hope it will receive the immediate support of all the states directly concerned with the pressing problem of the Middle East.
I am gratified to note that a statement has been released by the White House agreeing that a United Nations security council meeting of the character referred to by foreign minister Lloyd is clearly within the contemplation of the United Nations charter, and that if such a meeting were generally desired the United States would join in following this orderly procedure.
Yesterday I was able to say only that I was in personal and continuous consultation with Prime Minister Macmillan and President Eisenhower concerning this matter. The house will understand, too, that my guarded reference yesterday to the fact that the United Nations security council in session seemed to offer possibilities indicated at the same time that I was in full accord with both the purpose and the manner in which this initiative was being developed by the heads of government concerned. If we display that realism which is so necessary at this time I am confident that the way will be opened to these high level talks which the urgency of the matter demands.
While these negotiations leading to high level discussions have been going on, the security council's deliberations on Lebanon and Jordan have continued. At the meeting this morning the Soviet delegate proposed amendments to the Japanese draft resolution. I placed the terms of that resolution before the house yesterday, and I will not give any portion of it on this occasion. The amendments moved by the U.S.S.R. clearly changed the character of that resolution by calling for the condemnation of the United States action in regard to Lebanon and demanding an immediate withdrawal of United States forces.

External Affairs-Middle East
In view of the stand taken this morning by the Soviet representative I am led to believe- and I hope that my prophecy in this regard is not borne out by events-that the security council's efforts to bring about a solution to the immediate problem in Lebanon and Jordan will fail.
It is unfortunate that the position taken' by the Soviet union, if it is to be expected that the attitude of the U.S.S.R. will follow the speech made by its representative, will have the result of frustrating the efforts of the security council to take additional effective action in Lebanon.
However, under the terms of the existing security council resolution of June 11 there is some hope of action which can be taken immediately regardless of the outcome today of the deliberations of the security council on the Japanese resolution. On June 11, as hon. members know, a United Nations body- UNOGIL-was provided for and is still functioning in Lebanon. The latest reports from UNOGIL make it clear that the group is now able to expand its activities as the result of increasing access to the border areas.
I think this house realizes that this government has been co-operating actively in the development of UNOGIL, and has also given its firm support to the proposal to expand the activities of UNOGIL as contemplated under the terms of the Japanese resolution.
The secretary general informed the security council last week that 65 additional observers are required for the implementation of the existing resolution. I wish now to inform the house that, as requested by the secretary general, Canada will supply immediately three of the additional observers, of course giving every attention to any further requirement of UNOGIL as events transpire. If additional action in this regard is requested, not unfavourable consideration will be given to such requests.
As I see the situation at the moment, in view of the stand now taken by the United Kingdom and the United States of America on this matter, supported by Canada, the necessity of determining what further course will be taken now rests firmly with Mr. Khrushchev. Every opportunity has been provided to discuss immediately-providing the other nations agree-in the security council and within the ambit of the United Nations and under its auspices every problem connected with the Middle East, to the end that if there is agreement a solution can be found. I think the people of Canada as a whole will wholeheartedly support the stand this government is taking in this connection, which I believe carries with it the


support of the members of the opposition in this house as well as the country as a whole.
One can but express the hope that at this time Mr. Khrushchev, if sincere in his suggestions and the ideas he advanced in his several letters, will join with the nations of the free world in that institution to which he has given his support in those letters, in which letters he has warned mankind that there must be nothing done outside of the United Nations. He now definitely has the opportunity, providing that he is sincerely desirous to act, to react favourably to the initiative of the United Kingdom and the United States to bring about discussions which everyone hopes will lead to a solution.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house do indeed support the steps that have been taken and the progress that has been made as indicated by the Prime Minister to ensure-and it is important that it should be ensured-that there will not be a wholly negative reply given to the invitation of the head of the Soviet union government addressed to the four governments and the Secretary General of the United Nations to discuss the crisis in the Middle East.
If that can be done as has been suggested, by a special meeting of the security council attended by the heads of government, that I should think would be a satisfactory and welcome development. The charter of the United Nations does make provision for that kind of meeting, and in the past the Secretary General of the United Nations, Mr. Trygve Lie, worked quite hard to bring about a procedure by which foreign ministers and heads of government would attend security council meetings on important occasions. So this would be a fortunate development to meet a critical situation.
But, Mr. Speaker, if that particular form, a full council, were not considered to be satisfactory-and there are possible difficulties in regard to representation at the larger meeting, difficulties which I am sure occur to us at once-and if those difficulties were such that a meeting in the full council of the heads of government could not be arranged, I would certainly hope that this particular difficulty of representation would not be permitted to prevent a meeting of a somewhat different kind. Perhaps another way of doing it would be by a committee of the security council along the lines which I ventured to mention yesterday and which would certainly avoid that particular difficulty. It would retain the kind of representation which was advocated in the first proposal of the head of the Soviet government, and for that purpose would include India.

The important thing, Mr. Speaker, is not the mechanism; the important thing is to get the heads of the governments most concerned together to talk over the situation in the hope that by such discussion they might do something constructive to remove the cloud which hangs over international relations at the present time.
1 speak for our party when I tell the Prime Minister that we welcome the support the government has given to this move. We shall also support them in any move they make which will strengthen the position of the United Nations in Lebanon at the present time through strengthening the observer group there.
I was a little discouraged to read in the press this morning that the foreign minister of Lebanon had said that notwithstanding the presence of the United Nations observer group there and notwithstanding the intervention of the United States forces, intervention was still continuing undiminished across the border in the form of assistance to the rebels of that country. All this merely underlines that the sooner the powers most concerned can get together and do something to restore the political situation there the better it will be for peace not only in that area but in the whole world.

Mr. Speaker, members of this group are always very interested in reports the Prime Minister gives to the house with respect to this serious Middle East situation, and hope that his efforts to bring about a discussion will meet with the success for which we all wish.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, July 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Churchill for the second reading of Bill No. C-31, to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DELIVERY OF SEED GRAIN, MALTING BARLEY, ETC.
speechtext:
On July 16 I introduced this bill rather briefly, because it was then four minutes to six o'clock and I did not have the time to make the full explanation desirable. On page 2311 of Hansard for that date hon. members will find my introduction, which I will not repeat on this occasion, but I will bring up to date the figures relating to cash advances and the figures relating to quota deliveries.
With regard to cash advances my latest report is dated July 18, according to which the percentage refunded has reached 92.9 per cent, an indication that in the remaining days of July it is more than likely that the cash advances will be practically all repaid. Second, with regard to quota deliveries I stated on July 16 last that within a few days right across the prairies all the stations would be on 6- or 7-bushel delivery quota. Hansard has the word "years" where I used the word "days", which I corrected the following day. My prediction was correct; the wheat board now reports that of the 2,071 delivery points in the western provinces, 1,016 are on a 6-bushel quota, 1,023 are on a 7-bushel quota and there are 32 closed stations, indicating that the marketing of grain out west has gone ahead very well.
To proceed with my introduction to the amendments to this act, I have the following statement to make, and again this will be
2526	HOUSE OF
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act very brief. When the act was drafted last fall there were two or three omissions from the legislation which the proposed amendments are designed to correct. As the act now stands, a farmer who delivers malting barley is precluded from drawing an advance on his farm-stored wheat; similarly, deliveries of grain to be used for seeding purposes count against an advance. In the amendment we propose exempting deliveries of malting barley and of seed grain.
The third major amendment provides for the consolidation of cash advances from one crop year to the other. This will make it possible for a producer who has not fully repaid his cash advance through no fault of his own, which means because his quota has not been large enough to permit him to deliver or because there has been some difficulty for which he is not responsible, to obtain a further cash advance on his new crop year if desired. The two advances would then be consolidated and recorded in the permit book, and as quotas were raised the producer would repay both advances.
We do not anticipate that many producers will be affected by this provision, but we wish to guard any inconvenience to a producer who has grain to deliver and whose quota may be low. I have just pointed out that this is unlikely to affect very many people because, with two weeks to go for deliveries, cash advances have been repaid up to 92.9 per cent. Nevertheless we are introducing this amendment just to assist anyone who, through no fault of his own, might be subject to some inconvenience.

On that point, Mr. Chairman, last year when the bill was being considered for drafting one of the most important points was this very one raised this afternoon, as to what to do with regard to land in which perhaps two or three people have some interest. We tried to simplify the legislation last year, and we related it to the permit book. The permit book lists the owner of the land, the renter and all people who have an interest in it.
It was found necessary, relating cash advances to the permit book, that all those who had an interest in the land must then sign the application form if a cash advance was desired. It has caused some trouble to some people where the landlord was living far away or was unfamiliar with the legislation or not agreeable to signing the application form. All of that was very carefully considered. We reached the decision last year that we could not make provision for a cash advance based on the permit book to someone who was unable to obtain the signature of another or others who were also listed in that permit book.
Then this year we went through the same process again, and the most careful consideration was given to this problem. I asked the officials both here and those of the wheat board in Winnipeg to look at this again, and I have asked several hon. members of the house to produce a satisfactory solution to this problem. No one has come up with any good solution.
Let me just place on the record the considered opinion with regard to this matter. Section 6 of the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act requires joint application by all persons named in the same permit book before any advance will be made against grain deliverable under that permit book.

No distinction is made between a situation in which all or a substantial part of the land is subject to share interests by two or more persons, and the situation under which a substantial portion belongs outright to the actual producer and only part of the farm is subject to interests held by other persons. And finally, there is no means by which a tenant can compel a landlord or other interested persons to enter into a joint application.
The problems involved in joint applications, and the knowledge that they may give rise to delays, refusals to execute and so forth, were of considerable concern during the preparation of the legislation. The scheme underlying the act had, of course, recognized that grain stored on farms could not be inspected by competent persons as a condition precedent to entitlement for an advance. The time element and the number of persons required made this impossible. It also had to recognize that it would not be possible to impose some kind of requirement for segregation of the grain on which an advance was to be made, either segregation from all the grain stored by the farmer or segregation of the different portions of grain belonging to different interested persons.
The scheme also had to recognize that there are probably a multitude of ways in which an actual producer and his landlord, mortgagee or other type of producer divide their respective interests, and a multitude of forms of contract or other means as to how these shares were agreed upon or could be established or proved. It seemed an extremely difficult if not impossible task- other than by the various parties themselves confirming their private arrangement in a joint application form-to impose upon anyone to determine and satisfy himself just what were the true and accurate arrangements between the several interests in any given situation and in every situation.
Finally, partly because the permit book is the chief document to rely on to show past deliveries, and partly because it is the essential document in relation to recovery of the advance payment, the scheme had to be closely related to the permit book system. Under a scheme for cash advances against undelivered grain, however, the question of the respective shares of joint holders of a permit book becomes important and is exceedingly difficult.
This arises in three different aspects. First of all if, instead of the joint application principle now used, a joint holder was allowed to obtain an advance irrespective of the wishes, knowledge or interests of the other holders, 57071-3-160
22, 1958	2529
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act someone would have to know not only what grain there was behind his application but what his true share of that grain really was. It is difficult to see how this could be avoided, and it is difficult to know how the person making the advance could satisfy himself, without information or confirmation from the other interested persons, that the share stated by the applicant was correct.
This would be necessary for two reasons. The first is, of course, that since the advance is made and its amount is determined against grain that the applicant has and undertakes to deliver, he could only rightfully deliver his own true share, errors concerning its accuracy would greatly increase the dangers of overadvancing. Second, the total advances for any one permit book are limited by the grain to be delivered under that book. Hence if a single applicant overdraws by falsifying or misunderstanding the share of the grain to which he is entitled, the legitimate entitlement of other applicants under the same book would be reduced unless the over-all limit for any one farm unit is to be increased in such cases.
Another difficulty would arise in connection with the general lien created by section 10 of the act. At present, with the idea of joint applications the lien relates to all the grain in respect of which an advance payment is made, and in many cases this is probably coincident with most or all of the grain stored on the farm. If separate and independent applications were allowed this would, of course, require a change in the concept of the lien to cover only that share of the grain belonging to each individual applicant.
The third and perhaps the most important difficulty of all relates to the chief way in which advance payments are recovered. Under section 11 of the act, one half of the initial payment for grain delivered under a permit book is deducted and paid to the Canadian wheat board until the advance is fully recovered. This is obviously the best security that could be imposed. At present, with the requirement of joint applications, all grain delivered under the permit book is subject to this statutory deduction irrespective of whose grain is delivered. If individual advances were made in the case of joint permit books without any consent from the other holders, it would certainly be necessary to restrict this recovery provision to grain delivered by the individual recipient of the advance, and then only when he was delivering his own proper share of grain.
This would, I think, make it absolutely essential that the elevator operator receiving the grain-and the wheat board which is taking one half of the payment for itself- would need to be satisfied that the grain
2530	HOUSE OF
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act belonged to that person. If he were delivering some other holder's share I would think-[DOT] since the board in effect takes one half of it without any payment at the time of delivering -the board might be liable for conversion of another person's property.
The only practical means of meeting this problem, therefore, seems to be through a joint application signed by all parties possessing a joint interest in the grain as indicated in the individual permit books.
That, Mr. Chairman, constitutes the position we take after the most thorough consideration of this problem. When I made my introductory remarks on this bill I said that, based on another year's experience, if there are adjustments or changes that should be made we are quite prepared to do so provided they could be fitted into the general purpose of the act. As of this moment no one has produced the type of amendment which would meet this particular situation and, of course, the whole thing hinges on the question of what to do when a farmer is in default and who becomes liable. We tried to simplify the problem and related it to the permit book. So far it has worked extremely well, as the figures I gave earlier this afternoon indicate. The percentage of repayments is so close to being 100 per cent that the number of defaulters, if any, will be very limited and we will not face that problem of attempting to assess responsibility except in very few instances.
If too great a burden is placed upon a renter of land we have to get around this problem of responsibility in case of default, and I certainly am open to suggestions along that line. On the other hand, we are very close to a new crop year. We want to make it possible for advances to be made just as early as the farmers ask for them, and the only amendments which have been introduced on this occasion have dealt with the points that were chiefly under criticism during the last several months.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, all members who come from constituencies in the three prairie provinces are well aware of the fact that for many years past there have been a very large number of complaints with regard to anomalies and inequities which have been apparent as far as the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is concerned. Under the terms of the act as it has existed a great many of these have been inevitable. The purpose of these amendments is to remove, as far as it is possible to do so, the situations which have given rise to nearly all the complaints we have had in such large numbers in past years. It is proposed to do this by removing certain limitations in the act and a number of inequities in the method of making payment under the act.
Briefly, it is proposed to remove the six-section block limitation for areas with a low yield adjacent to eligible townships. This will have the effect of qualifying for payment, irrespective of township boundaries, any number of low yield sections in ineligible townships, provided they form a block with a side that is contiguous to an eligible township. It is also proposed to remove the six-section block limitation when excluding from payment high yield areas in eligible townships. The proposal is to exclude from payment any single section of land having a yield of 12 or more bushels, and also to exclude such sections from the computations in determining the category of payment. At present the high yield sections are included in computing the amount of award, and as a result the amount of award is not always commensurate with the yield in the payable area.
Another proposal is with regard to the minimum size of an eligible area. Up to date this has been an 18-section rectangular block. It is proposed to reduce the minimum area to be eligible for payment under the act to one third of a township, that is to a 12-section block rather than the 18 section block which has been in existence up to this time. This applies particularly to what has been known as C blocks, that is, blocks which may cover two, three or four townships.
The exclusion of certain crown lands granted after 1940 from benefits under the act is also considered discriminatory, and it is therefore proposed to repeal that section of the act so that no matter when the land 57071-3-160J
was granted by the crown it will be eligible for Prairie Farm Assistance Act payments.
A further proposal is to make flax and rape seed subject to the 1 per cent levy. Since the growers of such crops also benefit under this legislation it is felt that they, as well other farmers, should contribute to the prairie farm emergency fund. This was one of the quite apparent anomalies in the act. People growing flax and rape seed were eligible for benefits, but there was no levy imposed on their crops as there was on other crops.
Another change to be made is in the definition of "farmer" under the act. Up to date the definition of "farmer" in the act, and the way in which it was interpreted and spelled out in the regulations, provided that a man who had any other source of income or whose main source of income was as an elevator agent, school teacher or some other form of occupation and who also operated a farm was ineligible to receive any award under the act. It is proposed to change the definition of "farmer" in order to remedy that situation, and also to change the regulations. Therefore when this particular amendment is passed and the regulations are changed anyone who operates a farm, except a corporation, will be eligible to receive an award under the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: That would cover a tenant, I presume.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Yes. Tenants, of course, have always been eligible. Anyone operating a farm has been eligible unless he had some other form of business. For example, a large number of elevator agents in western Canada also have quarter or half sections which they farm in the same way any other farmers does; but because they were elevator agents and had a steady source of income they were not eligible to receive payment although they had to pay into the fund. The 1 per cent levy was taken from them. These people will now become eligible. It is not proposed to make eligible corporations such as insurance companies, mortgage companies and so on which may have repossessed land as a result of a lien they had on it.
Another change has to do with flooding. Through the years there has been a considerable amount of complaint in areas where flooding takes place that it was extremely difficult for a farmer whose land was flooded to be eligible unless he was in a very widespread flood area. These complaints came from farmers who suffered from flooding, and who felt that the minimum area necessary to qualify was too large. At present there must be a flooded area of at least one sixth
2532	HOUSE OF
Prairie Farm Assistance Act of a township or 3,840 cultivated acres before the farmers can qualify. That figure does not mean simply that much acreage, but that much cultivated acreage. It is proposed to reduce this acreage by making eligible any area consisting of six or more adjoining sections of land where at least one-third of the cultivated acreage is flooded. In other words, eligibility as far as flooding is concerned will be reduced so that if you have any block of six sections that may run along the course of a river and one-third of the cultivated land in those six sections is flooded, then those farmers will be eligible for awards under the act.
Another matter that has caused a great deal of complaint is in those areas where little wheat is grown. Under the act as it is at the present time awards have been made on the basis solely of the damage to the wheat crop. You would have cases in which there would be perhaps only 40 acres or 50 acres of wheat in a whole township of 36 sections, but nevertheless the determination of what the award should be for P.F.A. payment was made on that small amount of wheat. It is proposed to put into effect an amendment which will provide that in any eligible area in which the percentage of wheat seeded is less than 10 per cent, then the predominant crop-oats, barley or rye-may be taken as the crop to be used as the one to determine what the eligibility for award will be.
Those are the main changes in the act or the main amendments which are proposed. There are several others of lesser importance whose purpose is largely to facilitate the administration of the act and which, without the act being before hon. members, I do not think it would be profitable for me to go into at this time.
As I have already indicated, of course, In addition to these amendments it is proposed to revise the regulations established under the act so that they will be in accordance with the amendments which have been made. In some cases the regulations will be changed, although no actual change is being made in any particular section of the act, in order to liberalize the administration of the legislation.
I should just like to say one further word, Mr. Chairman. There is some urgency in getting these amendments through in view of the widespread drought conditions which exist in western Canada this year and which mean that what acreage there is in some areas will be ripening up earlier than usual. Therefore it will be necessary to start the P.F.A.A. program this year earlier than is normal. As a result, it is highly desirable


to have this legislation completed in the house as soon as possible so that then there will be time to have the regulations amended, and then to have the necessary new forms which will be required printed and distributed so that everything will be ready to put the program into operation very soon after the end of this month.

That is right. In the meantime my hon. friend's officials, of course, could anticipate the passage of this legislation by making the necessary amendments in the regulations and at least have that much work ahead of them.
The amendments which are proposed have been indicated in a general way by the minister who has spoken in the committee stage on the resolution. While these amendments in the regulations and at least have that vantages, I think the minister would agree that they are not of a fundamental kind but rather are designed to extend the legislation by simplifying some of the regulations and making it possible to be more generous and more flexible in the granting of assistance. This legislation, of course, makes its appeal to those of us who sit on this side of the house because we have had a long association with this particular measure the purpose of which I think could be described by saying that it was to assist in the rehabilitation of drought and soil drifting areas in the prairie provinces and to provide greater security and stability for agriculture generally.
The basic legislation was passed in 1935. It provided for the payment out of the federal exchequer of some $4.75 million over a five-year period. In 1937 an amendment to this basic act was drafted extending the scope of the program. Provision was made to resettle farmers on better land and poor lands were withdrawn from cultivation and placed under pasture.

speechtext: That had nothing to do with it. That was under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.

Yes, I know. But nevertheless it had a basic and kindred result,

as my hon. friend so well knows. A subsequent amendment providing for this legislation, of course, dealt with many of the features in principle that are already contemplated by my hon. friend. I suppose it would be true to say that the basic purpose of this legislation is to compensate for crop failure due to drought, as my hon. friend has said. He has pictured the condition that earns it. However, it has also been used in compensation for hail and other natural hazards for which it was primarily intended. It is now suggested, I think, by those who have spent a good deal of time in studying this particular type of project that the reason why it has not proved completely satisfactory for all the purposes for which it had been applied was that it was used extensively, as I have said, for hail and other natural hazards. It may be that on this account the rigidity has been unduly severe because it is easier to define areas of drought, I suppose, than it is to define areas of hail. I suggest that the legislation before us today might be indicated somewhat by the observations made by the present Prime Minister and by the Minister of Agriculture himself. It may be that some of the suggestions that were made by the Prime Minister in 1957 are being incorporated in the present bill. In any event, we can ascertain that matter when the particulars of the bill are brought before us. However, as reported at page 1472 of Hansard of February 20, 1957, the Prime Minister said:
My suggestions as to other amendments that might be made are these. First, while the placing of indemnities on an individual farm basis may be impractical, consideration should be given, as far as possible, to the amendment of the act to provide for the payment of indemnity on a section basis.
I am not sure whether or not that is the kind of amendment that my hon. friend has spoken of in a general way. However, it will be very interesting, when we come to the bill, to see whether or not the Prime Minister's desires of 1957 when sitting on this side of the house are now incorporated in the amendment. Then as reported at 1473 of Hansard the Prime Minister said this:
The question of crop insurance is one that requires a great deal of investigation. If one reads the report of the Saskatchewan commission on rural questions and the report of the Manitoba royal commission one has some idea of the immensity of the problem and all the difficulties inherent in introducing in our country legislation analogous to that in the United States. While I realize that this parliament is now rapidly approaching its end and it is only a matter of a few weeks before it will cease to exist, even now the committee on agriculture might be convened in order to hear representations, consider recommendations and come to a general decision on this very important matter, for sooner or later it has to be faced.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act That is the matter of crop insurance. The legislation which my hon. friend has indicated and of which the house is now seized does not, of course, deal with crop insurance, and one is inclined to strongly agree with the suggestion made by the present Prime Minister when he was leader on this side of the house that this matter is one which it is becoming increasingly important to face. The Prime Minister went on to say at this time: Third, I suggest that the regulations now in existence should be revamped to a considerable extent.
He does not indicate the extent to which regulations should be amended, but it is possible that some of the amendments about which my hon. friend spoke a few moments ago are along the general lines indicated by the then member for Prince Albert, who was leader of the opposition at the time and who, at page 1473 of Hansard for February 20, 1957, continued as follows:
I believe that is necessary and I believe that if the committee on agriculture were set up even at this late date suggestions and recommendations could be made by the committee which would lay a foundation for the establishment of a crop insurance plan.
The Minister of Agriculture, who was then the member for Calgary North, said at page 1482 of Hansard for the same date:
I would hope that when the act is being amended the minister will take the opportunity to correct some of the injustices as far as payments are concerned. I refer particularly to Indians.
I do not know whether my hon. friend has the Indians in mind or not, because he did not indicate that in his main statement, but undoubtedly when we get to the bill we will have the opportunity to learn whether it has been possible for the government to bring forward legislation along the lines which the minister at that time thought desirable.

I thank my hon. friend. Then the minister went on to say: Another group of people whom I can see no reason for excluding are those covered by section 3 of the act, subsection 3 of which reads as follows: "3. No award under this section shall be made-" And this is under paragraph (c) (i).

The minister continues:
Why people who hold land under the Soldier Settlement Act or under the Veterans' Land Act should be excluded from the benefits of this act I quite fail to understand. It seems to be another case of gross discrimination for which there is no excuse. I would make a very strong plea to the minister that he remove that exclusion from the benefits of this act as far as people holding land under the Veterans' Land Act are concerned. As a matter of fact the amount of land any veteran was able to get under the Veterans' Land Act was .a small farm, not sufficient to put him in farming in a very big way. They are among the very group of farmers who on the whole perhaps need the assistance or help they can get under a scheme of this kind more than do farmers generally.
There followed some interjections on which 1 do not need to dwell, but these were some of the views expressed by the minister at that time and it will be interesting to know whether it has been possible for him to carry out his recommendations. I know whether he has or has not carried out this particular recommendation he will deal with it very frankly, as is his usual practice, when we deal with the bill.
I think this is the moment to reiterate what I know has been stated by some hon. gentlemen opposite to the effect that benefits of this legislation should, of course, at some time or other and given the necessary conditions, be made applicable not only to particular sections of Canada but to all parts of the country. I am speaking now for myself and I would say that any legislation which is of benefit to one section of the country but which is capable of application in terms of benefit to all parts of the nation should be made to apply to the nation as a whole and it will be very interesting to have the minister's observations on this suggestion.
It may be that the most effective way of dealing with the matter is to respond to the request now being made, according to my information, by a growing number of people all over the country for the establishment of a nation-wide system of crop insurance. This view is one which has been expressed by my leader, who proposed a national system of crop insurance generally financed by the provincial and federal authorities with municipal assistance in respect of its administration.
It seems to me the time has now come to urge the convocation of a federal, provincial and municipal conference to discuss the possibility of such a scheme and to set experts to work preparing for it. I hesitate to suggest such a meeting between the federal and provincial governments because _ of the great difficulty we have had in getting the federal government to reconvene the meeting with the provinces in respect to fiscal matters, but it may be that we could bring about that important result by these ad hoc arrangements, one of which was provided by


the Minister of Labour the other day when municipalities, management and labour met with the departments of labour of the various provincial governments and with the federal Minister of Labour in order to discuss the important matter of unemployment.
As I said a moment ago, this matter of crop insurance seems to me to be increasingly capturing the attention of a large section of the public and in view of the heavy contributions made by the Canadian taxpayers generally to groups of Canadians of various occupations for one reason or another, it seems to me that in the matter of crop failures due to acts of God and the like, this might be regarded as a very effective way of providing the kind of assistance needed.
I do not know if the Minister of Agriculture recalls this, but I was very interested in some correspondence I had with him and a very frank telephone conversation between us on the matter of the great damage suffered by farmers in a certain section of Canada which will not be affected by this legislation. These farmers suffered the loss of millions of dollars as a result of crop damage due to very serious damage by hail stones. This was in a section of the country in the east and, based upon statements made in the election campaign of 1957 to the effect that the federal government would provide assistance for such crop failure, I had written to the Prime Minister reminding him of his promise through one of his spokesmen during that election. I pointed out the nature of the damage and the millions of dollars loss suffered by the farmers and I asked him to implement his pledge. The Prime Minister replied saying that the matter would be looked into and at the same time one member of this house who comes from my section of the country made an announcement that the matter was also being looked into by the government of the province of Ontario. We have heard nothing more of this, and the province of Ontario has not acted.
Then I confronted the Minister of Agriculture who, quite properly, pointed out that there were constitutional practices in this country and that as long as he was Minister of Agriculture the responsibility for looking after individuals should be shared in the way I have indicated-that they should be looked after first by their own municipality and then if the municipality was unable to help, by the province. Only then, in his judgment, could it be expected that assistance would be provided by the federal government. As I say, I think that is a correct statement of the constitutional practice.
But that is not what was said by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe who was the

spokesman for the government on that occasion in the town of Essex when the farmers in that area were assured that the government would come to their assistance in the event that their crops suffered as a result of storms or acts of God.
So in order that we may deal finally with situations of this sort, possibly the minister could find occasion during the discussion of this bill to indicate what the government's intentions or thoughts may be with regard to crop insurance generally. It would be a relevant matter to discuss in respect to the amendments being provided to this bill, a bill which undoubtedly has given much satisfaction and contributed considerably to the well-being of the farmers of the prairie provinces.

We appreciate the fact that the zoning has been changed, thereby eliminating the rigidity that formerly existed with regard to the large township areas, and we think that much good will accrue to farmers who are in an area on the boundary of a good area and who were in the past eliminated from the possibility of obtaining assistance under this act.

Mr. Chairman, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has certainly been very helpful in the past to the prairie farmers. I have a few observations to make about the advantages of that legislation, which has been of real benefit to farmers in western Canada.
This legislation was enacted to give assistance to farmers who suffered damage as a result of drought, floods and other natural causes. Eastern farmers are in favour of the measure but would like it extended to the whole of Canada.
Eastern farmers, like western farmers, suffer damage from those same causes. In fact, I remember that last year some farmers in my neighbourhood lost their entire crop as a result of a storm. Not only did they lose their crop but their farm buildings also suffered considerable damage, such as broken windows, and so on, and some of their cattle were injured. In short, after the storm they had absolutely nothing left, not even enough potatoes or vegetables for their own use. Therefore, they lost the fruit of a whole year's work and consequently were very badly off financially. It is for that reason that we would like to see that legislation extended to the whole of Canada.
Like the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), I would like to see crop insurance inserted in that legislation. I know that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) has referred to this many times in January, February and March before farmers organizations. In fact, he said at the time that he would introduce legislation on crop insurance. Unfortunately, the house has yet to hear about it. In my opinion, the minister had an excellent opportunity to elaborate on this project when he introduced his amendment, because I believe that crop insurance would be complementary to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
We urge the minister to take this into consideration; in putting forward these recommendations, I am expressing, I believe, the views of our eastern farmers.

Also, as I say, there is a very clear indication that a severe inequity exists in that most of the lands granted after 1940 were not sub-marginal lands but land that is among the best producing land in the three prairie provinces.

There is no doubt but that the extreme variability of climatic conditions across Canada makes the matter of a general dominion-wide crop insurance scheme an extraordinarily difficult problem to solve. However, as I say, we are working on it in the department and I hope that in the near future we can introduce legislation in respect of a crop insurance scheme.
Another statement made by the hon. member for Essex East which was also referred to by other hon. members was that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act should be extended to all parts of Canada. In that regard I would merely point out that the great difficulty is how to make the levy. How would
you collect the payment the farmer makes in connection with this? As far as the three prairie provinces are concerned it is very easy because grain is all handled through the wheat board. The levy is deducted by the wheat board and paid into the fund by the board and so it is a very simple matter to make collection of the levy but in any other part of Canada the question of collecting the levy from the farmer comparable to the 1 per cent levy collected on western grain would present very great difficulties as I think hon. members will readily appreciate. It would be an almost impossible practice to put into operation particularly as most agricultural producers in other parts of Canada derive the major portion of their livelihood through livestock or livestock products rather than through crops as is the case in western Canada.
That is one of the great difficulties as far as extending this particular scheme to other parts of the country is concerned. I do not think it would be a practical proposition. That is another reason why I think we should have a system of crop insurance.
The hon. member for Essex East also referred to certain damage that took place in an area of his own constituency. All I can say in regard to that is I do not know what statements the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe may have made prior to the 1957 election but, as the hon. member himself said, he is well aware of the fact that damage to a small area or damage to an individual has always been and must be, under our constitutional system and practice, looked upon as the responsibility of the municipality and of the province and then if it is damage of such an extensive nature that the province is not able to handle the matter, it applies to the dominion government for assistance. This was done in the case of the Red river flood at Winnipeg; it was done in the case of the Cabano fire and in various other instances, but the matter of expecting-I do not think the hon. member himself really does expect it-the dominion government to come in and pay damages of individual farmers in a small area is something that would be hopeless and impossible for us to do.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIMITS ON COMPENSATION FOR SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act to remove the statutory limits on the amount of compensation for cattle slaughtered pursuant to the act, except when slaughtered pursuant to area or herd disease eradication programs, in which case the limits are to be increased.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Rea in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIMITS ON COMPENSATION FOR SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of the bill to be introduced is to amend the rates of compensation for cattle ordered slaughtered as a disease control measure under the authority of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. As the act now stands, compensation is authorized at their market value for all classes of livestock except horses and cattle. In the case of cattle there is a statutory limitation on compensation at a maximum of $100 for purebred animals and $40 for grade animals.
There are two types of circumstances under which cattle may be ordered slaughtered
Animal Contagious Diseases Act and compensation paid. One has to do with spasmodic outbreaks of serious diseases which do not normally exist in Canada such as the foot-and-mouth outbreak in 1952. It is desirable that the owners of animals slaughtered in such instances should be compensated at market value. That has not been the case up to date. All cattle were compensated for at the regular rates laid down which I have just indicated.
The other circumstance under which cattle may be ordered slaughtered and compensation paid has to do with area or herd programs for the eradication of diseases which are established in Canada. Examples of that are the tuberculosis eradication program and the recently instituted one for area testing and eradication of brucellosis.
It is not considered necessary or desirable to compensate owners at full market value for cattle ordered slaughtered under such programs, but the maximum compensations now permitted by the act are felt to be inadequate under present conditions. I might say that these limits were established quite a number of years ago and since that time prices of cattle generally have increased. Therefore it is felt to be only fair and reasonable that the rates of compensation should be increased in a way somewhat commensurate with the increase in the price of cattle.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIMITS ON COMPENSATION FOR SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext: When were the basic rates fixed?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIMITS ON COMPENSATION FOR SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
The basic rates were fixed shortly after the first war. It just happens that at that period cattle were a relatively good price. Otherwise the rate of compensation would have been extraordinarily badly out of line with the price of cattle during recent years.
The effect of the present bill will be to permit the payment of compensation at market value for cattle ordered slaughtered in the control of spasmodic outbreaks of serious diseases and to raise the maximum compensation under the tuberculosis and brucellosis eradication programs to $140 for purebred cattle and $70 for grades. I might say that the bill is a very simple one of one clause for the purpose of increasing the rates of compensation as far as cattle are concerned under the herd testing programs.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIMITS ON COMPENSATION FOR SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the increase for purebred cattle is to $140. I do not know whether the minister is aware that for some few years now the price of purebred cattle has been from $400 to $1,000 for good purebred cows. I wonder whether the minister would consider increasing the amount from $140. The same holds true in the case of grade cattle. If you want to buy a reasonably

good cow today you have to pay $150 to $250 but under this legislation farmers will only get $70 when cows have to be slaughtered. I think the minister should consider increasing the amounts to $125 for grade cows and to $200 or $250 for purebred cows. When a farmer loses his cows he has to buy others and he is not able to replace the slaughtered cows.

subtopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, July 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Broome for the second reading of Bill No. S-6, respecting Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company.

subtopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
On Friday last, Mr. Speaker, I was drawing my remarks to a close at six o'clock and I have but one or two other comments to make on this bill. The house will recall that I had just entered the phase of my discussion that dealt with the representations that had been made to those of us in the C.C.F. by the officials of this company and the admission by the officials that probably one of the main reasons why the stock rose from its original value of $10 to something in the neighbourhood of $140 was that they did not place on the market more of the original shares which they had in the treasury. The opinion was expressed that perhaps if the company, in the first instance, had allowed for the sale of more of their original 5 million shares on the market the price of the shares would not have gone as high as it did and they would not have had to come to parliament last year and again this year asking for a five-to-one split.
We have a number of questions which must be answered but unfortunately I do not think the officials of the company can answer them, for certainly those officials have no control over the movement of share prices on the market. There is no guarantee by the officials of the company that if this stock split is allowed under the present system of selling shares the general public will get an opportunity to participate in buying more shares. There is no guarantee

that these shares will not be offered privately to the same oil companies that now have the bulk of the shares in Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. There is no assurance either as to what will happen when the stock split takes place. Past records will show that when a stock split has taken place in other companies there has been a tendency for the price to go up again to what it was before the stock split took place. We have no assurance at all that this rise in price will not develop again and that the public interest will not be unprotected.
As we submitted earlier in 1951 when this company was originally incorporated and as we submit now, there is only one way in which to protect the interest of the public with respect to the operation of this particular oil pipe line and with respect to its sister organization the gas pipe line and that is to classify them as utilities and operate them under public ownership so that the public gets the fullest possible benefits from the operation of that profitable industry.
Those are my remarks, Mr. Speaker. It is true that they have been spread over three different days and that a number of questions have been raised. I am sure the bill will pass second reading. When it gets to the committee the members who are on the committee will have an opportunity of raising these questions with the officials of the company who are there. I hope that they will undertake to elicit information about these questions that have been raised and will undertake, as best they possibly can- inasmuch as the company is not publicly owned-to ensure that the interests of the general public will be protected all across the board.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

subtopic: AMENDMENT REQUIRING RETURNS SHOWING INCOMES OF POLITICAL PARTIES
AMENDMENT REQUIRING RETURNS SHOWING INCOMES OF POLITICAL PARTIES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-18, to amend the Canada Elections Act (election expenses).
He said: First, I must express my appreciation, Mr. Speaker, to the hon. member who seconded my motion for second reading. I refer to the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis). As outlined in the explanatory notes, the purpose of the bill is as outlined in the explanatory notes. Basically it is this. The Canada Elections Act at the moment, as hon. members know, provides that each candidate must file with the returning officer in his constituency a return setting out the sources of income for that candidate's campaign and also setting out the expenditures that are made on behalf of that candidate in respect of advertising, transportation and similar related costs in the conduct of the election. Unfortunately, though, the act at the moment does not make any provision for the declaration of income or expenditures by the central parties themselves.
We all know very well what happens. A candidate in declaring the source of his income-which I think must be properly treated as public information-can hide the true source if he has knowledge of it, or if he has not knowledge of it he can merely indicate that part of the contribution to his election campaign came from a central party headquarters, no matter which party it might be. The purpose behind the bill, as I said, is to provide that the national party headquarters, the national office of the particular political party, also be required to make a return indicating the source of their income, the amount, and whether it is in cash or whether it is as payment by some other outside group for services rendered to that particular party's operations.
I will undertake to get some statistical material as it relates to the province of British Columbia from returns filed by candidates in that province representing all of the political parties which ran candidates. We have from the province of British Columbia, of course, only two of those parties represented here in the house at the present time. It is not my desire to place on the record the source of income as declared by each individual candidate, whether or not he be elected.
One of the interesting things which was discovered as a result of this information, which incidentally is available to any member of the general public who wants to pay 20 cents in order to get it, was that with respect to the Conservative party and Liberal
Canada Elections Act
party declarations of sources of income, the major portion of the contributions to the campaign of an individual candidate was listed as coming from party headquarters. As far as the Conservatives were concerned, the figures ran in amounts such as $4,500, $10,000, $6,000, $7,000, $5,000 and so on. The major portion of contributions to the campaign of individual Conservative candidates in the province of British Columbia are listed anywhere from $4,000 up to $10,000 and the source is declared as either the Progressive Conservative party provincial headquarters or a private accounting company by the name of Field and Company in Vancouver, which was probably a bookkeeping agency hired by the Conservatives in order to keep track of the vast amount of money which they received in order to operate the last election.
The main issue is that there is no compulsion under the act for the candidate to declare the source, because he may not know where the money originated, but also that there is no compulsion on the central party to indicate where it gets these thousands and thousands of dollars with which to run a campaign. Certainly if political parties are to operate to the best interests of the general public then there must be an accounting to the general public as to the source of campaign fund contributions. If it is equitable that a candidate must declare the names of individuals or companies from whom he receives contributions and the amount of such contributions, then it is equitable that the national party itself should make a similar declaration to the general public as to the source of its income. We all know, I am sure, of the bible phrase, "Where your treasure lies there lies your heart also."
One of the unfortunate parts of the operation of elections here in Canada and even more so in the United States is that large industrial concerns and financial corporations, huge monopoly or semi-monopoly interests which want to ensure that the party forming the government will be partial to their ideas can easily and probably do make contributions in large amounts of money towards the campaign of any particular party. I am not saying because they make these contributions that any particular party will perform some sort of skulduggery to ensure that legislation passed is in the interests of the people who make such contributions, but it naturally follows that the party concerned will look upon those who contribute to it as friends and that the legislation it passes will be drafted with this in mind.
The general public, in the long run, pays for every political contribution made, whether

Canada Elections Act
it be to the Tories or to the Liberals. It is made by large business concerns but the general public in one way or another pays, in the final analysis, for all contributions made to the so-called free enterprise parties. Therefore the general public should have an accounting as to the source of such income. Without going into too much detail this is purely and simply an expansion of the principle already laid-down in the act as it applies to individual candidates. Certainly if it is just that a candidate must show to the general public the sources from which he gets his campaign contributions it is equally just that the central parties make a similar declaration.
I rather expect, Mr. Speaker, that in the ensuing moments before six o'clock some other hon. members may have some comments to make on this bill, which I do hope will be given the support of the house. We all know from past experience that public bills in the hands of private members have very little chance of speedy passage through the house; invariably discussion is still going on at six o'clock and a vote is not taken on the bill. However, as I expressed myself on another bill standing in my name, which has been dealt with and which has not yet been voted upon by this house, I am not adverse to deferring second reading of this bill and having the subject referred to the committee on privilege and elections where it could be discussed and studied in more detail than is possible in committee of the whole house.

subtopic: AMENDMENT REQUIRING RETURNS SHOWING INCOMES OF POLITICAL PARTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has covered this subject very completely, and he has set forth several suggestions that I intended to put forth myself. In the few minutes that are available I hope I will not repeat too much of what he has put forward. This subject is one which is obviously prominent in the minds of hon. members because most of us have been through two elections within the past year. This refers not only to the expenses which the member himself has incurred but to those which the party has incurred as well.
I wonder whether this bill is aimed at the contributors or at the party? Perhaps it is a little of both. I think that if it is aimed at the contributor it is an effort perhaps to pin him down. Perhaps it is well known that some contributors manage to contribute to two or more parties. Theoretically there is nothing basically wrong with that if the contributor feels that it is his duty to see that the platforms and the literature of all the parties are put forward equally, but that is the theoretical basis. I think the practical basis is -and I think this is what the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) has in mind-that perhaps some of those contributors, in supporting two or more parties, are just playing it safe. I believe they are perfectly entitled to do so if they feel that this will achieve what they expect. However, this brings up the second question to which I wish to refer. If there is any suggestion that those contributions amount to something corrupt or that practices coming from them are contrary to public morals, then I would say there is something to be concerned about; but there is no suggestion-at least I heard nothing in the introduction of the bill-that there is

Canada Elections Act
corruption and therefore it is not necessary to go ahead on the basis that we must pin those people down.
I feel that any legislation which tends to limit the rights of the public to do as they like, any legislation that tends to regulate what a person may do in general terms, must be justified. This is an instance of regulating the contributions that a contributor may make to a political party in the same way, as mentioned by the hon. member for Edmonton West, as revealing his vote or finding out which party he supports. Any such legislation that restricts or regulates the rights of private individuals or corporations must have some justification and must be necessary in the public interest, before this house should see fit to carry it.
There is another matter. That concerns the definition of a political party. The bill makes no attempt to define a political party in a manner which would meet a good many of the situations which arise. We know that in this house there are three recognized political parties. I would suggest that in the case of these three parties perhaps they can be readily identified and their national headquarters can be identified; but there are many people who run in an election under a variety of party names. If one person forms his own party and runs, is he a political party or is he merely an individual? I think that he is not a political party at all. Let us suppose, that two or more people are running on a similar ticket with a similar name. Would they become a political party? I think there is a possibility that they might be. There are always a number of people who run, as far at least as their public declarations are concerned, as independents. I think we must recognize that there is no independent party, as such, and therefore all the people who call themselves independent I submit should not be recognized as a party.

speechtext:
It seems that, when the time comes around for federal elections, a certain number of contributors always turn up at the right moment and provide what are referred to as "the sinews of war", and the campaign is on.
As for the bill proposed by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), I recognize that it is no doubt inspired by a certain spirit of idealism, which I cannot criticize and I therefore congratulate the hon. member for bringing about a discussion on the contribution of electoral funds. However, I do not believe that the bill will accomplish its purpose, since it purports to change, as it were, to a certain degree, human nature itself.
There is already in the Canada Elections Act a parallel to the bill now proposed by the hon. member for Skeena. I mean the report which all candidates are required to fill as regards contributions received and expenses incurred. However, in spite of all the precautions taken in the Elections Act to give a definition of numerous offences, often subject to very serious penalties, everybody

admits that the reports filled in by candidates and their official agents, as to their expenses, are not complete.
I do not say that candidates or their agents send in reports which are deliberately inaccurate, but there are a thousand and one ways of eluding that provision of the act which, for all practical purposes, becomes inoperative and, in my view, encourages a certain hypocrisy.
Hon. members also know that many expenses specifically prohibited by the Elections Act are made just the same, not by the candidates or their official agents, but by other people who take part in elections and spend money for purposes which, under the act, are illegal. We know it and I believe that if this bill goes through, the same situation would prevail. The parties would, as a matter of form, send in reports stating amounts of official contributions. However, beside this official accounting, there would be an unofficial accounting, and a large number of contributions would not be accounted for.
I also feel that we should oppose this bill for the sake of public morality. If it went through, it would indeed give many people an opportunity to violate an explicit provision of the Elections Act. That is, in my view, one of the objectionable features of this bill. There are of course many others minutely described earlier by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert).
I think it would be impossible in practice to apply this legislation. That is why, in spite of all the statutes that are enacted, the matter of electoral funds and expenses, not only of political parties, but of candidates, is always surrounded with mystery. Despite the inadequacy of the present system, there have been no suggestions of dishonesty or evidence of contributions made for the express purpose of illegally obtaining political advantages after the elections.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would you please put the motion? Would you read it, please?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
It is moved by Mr. Martin (Essex East):
14. That the excise tax on motor vehicles he repealed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that amendment is so clearly out of order that I find it difficult to speak with restraint-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -when it is put forward by a member who has been in the house now for nearly 20 years and yet puts forward an amendment as completely and clearly out of order as that one.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Why don't you speak to the point of order?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Every member knows perfectly well that no such amendment may be moved, except by a member of the government, as it affects the balance of ways and means and consequently, like all the resolutions contained in the budget, requires the royal recommendation. This matter does not even require discussion. It is so palpably and obviously an attempt to circumvent the rules of the house for what is thought to be a political advantage.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to deal with the last observation made by the Minister of Finance. He knows perfectly well that there is a duty on those of us on this side of the house to do what we think is in the interests of the nation and of our constituents. I could well ask you, Mr. Chairman, to ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw what he said but I am not going to. The hon. gentleman said that he spoke in reply to my proposal with restraint.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not in reply; I was speaking on the point of order.

Many of us had occasion within the last few minutes to give careful consideration to the desirability of restraint with regard to procedural matters that have taken place in a most unusual way in this house tonight.
We did not ask for a flag.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on the point of order-
Sit down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-before my hon. friend tears any more of the rules of the house to shreds and tatters it might be well

Excise Tax Act
to remind him that it is completely out of order to reflect on the vote of any hon. member of the house.
You cannot raise a point of order on a point of order.

My hon. friend, of course, dismisses the right of an hon. member to take the course I have taken by using a series of adjectives, none of which, of course, was based in any way upon the rules of the house. My hon. friend did not refer Your Honour to any rule of the house. He simply said that it was so obvious that my motion was out of order that it required no comment except the whole series of characteristic adjestives that flowed from the lips of my hon. friend. I refer Your Honour to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, 1958, No. 265 on page 221, which is in these words:
No member other than a minister of the crown may introduce a bill for the reduction of duties. The government must take full responsibility for the taxation levied to provide the revenue. But the house-
I would call these words to Your Honour's attention.
____enjoys complete freedom to make every representation possible to the government with regard to the manner in which the ministers discharge this responsibility.
I will make no comment about the implications of that with respect to the right of those of us on this side or in any quarter of the house to discuss the taxation policy of the government, but I would call Your Honour's attention particularly to the final sentence.
This duty the members may perform by moving amendments to reduce the taxes proposed by the administration.

I say that the most obvious of the inadequacies which make it most inexpedient for us to be asked to do this is the total failure of the government to do anything about the excise tax on motor cars which is imposed under this act.

I shall endeavour to comply with the increasing limitations and restrictions imposed by this government, which went to the country to restore the rights of parliament-
Order.
Closure.

-and which is now exhibiting what it meant by restoring the rights of parliament. Surely what British parliamentary history was about was the right of the House of Commons to decide what imposts should be imposed upon the people. Here

we have a Minister of Finance with the arrogance to say that what he says is expedient we have got to accept as expedient without any question, that we cannot discuss whether he has chosen the right way or the wrong way to do this, that we simply have to rubber stamp this limited, inadequate list of things totally at variance with what the minister promised from one end of the country to the other in two general elections. In other words, sir, the word "expedient" in any dictionary that I have ever looked at, if it means anything, means "advisable".
This course is advisable or it is not advisable. Surely it is impossible to discuss that matter without discussing alternatives. As I say, it seems to me that since the most important perhaps of any of the imposts in the public mind imposed under this tax-and one which, incidentally, the government promised either to take off or substantially reduce

is not comprehended within this resolution, it makes a mockery of parliament, of our procedure-
Oh, oh.
-and of our whole parliamentary procedure if we are to be gagged and circumscribed in this fashion.
Oh, oh.

speechtext: Order. I must ask the hon. member to come back to this resolution of the amendment and not to wander away from it quite as much as he has done.

I want to ask the Minister of Finance if he thinks that the public will be satisfied and will consider it an expedient thing to do to remove the sales tax on chimneys instead of removing it on motor cars, particularly as this tax is not even being removed on all chimneys but only on chimneys not in fireplaces.
What about rat poison?
This is just a start.
Moreover, if the minister thinks that ash handling-
What is going on now?

I forbear to make the obvious reference to ash handling, Mr. Chairman. If the minister thinks that the removal of the sales tax on ash handling and fuel handling equipment-I suppose the fuel handling equipment is to lift coal that is no longer being mined in Nova Scotia-will satisfy the public. If the minister thinks that the public will think this is as good as taking the tax off motor cars, I think the minister had better not go back to the public again for a while.
You should know.

Then, of course, perhaps he has come a little bit nearer to what would be expected when he proposes to take the tax off fuel oil tanks for use with furnaces for the heating of buildings and connected directly to such furnaces. But now here is one that will certainly give a thrill to the average man who expected the cost of motor cars to be reduced. This is something that is going to give him a thrill when he finds that the sales tax is going to be taken off latch sets, master key cylinder blocks, knobs and hinges.
Is there anything about bubble gum?

Then, Mr. Chairman, we come to something that I think will have an almost universal appeal from cape Bonavista right to Estevan point. The tax is to be taken off hard surface plastic laminated building materials. I have no doubt that it is a very good thing to take the tax off these things. I have no objection to it whatsoever. But I suggest that it is a rather inadequate substitute for what before the election-and particularly before the election a year ago-the public were told they could expect from hon. gentlemen who are now sitting on the treasury benches.
What about bubble gum?

Then we have another one. The tax is to be taken off underlayment material for hard surface floor coverings for permanent bonding to floors. Of course, the sex appeal of that is evident to every hon. member and it will no doubt have a tremendous appeal to the people of Canada. Then finally we have this one:
(viii) Articles and materials to be used exclusively in the manufacture of the foregoing.
