I am only too happy to leave the Minister of Finance to his own rat poison. These are apparently all the repeals. Then we have the second section which is certainly the kind of section that a person who wanted to buy a motor vehicle at a lower price than he is now paying would find more than adequate as compensation for his disappointment.
What did your government do?
Oh, good heavens, Mr. Chairman; good heavens.
That staggers you.

We are in this house to debate the ambit of this resolution and the hon. member, the aspirant for the position of parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, now proposes to debate the record of the previous government. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, in raising such an issue he is out of order.
I suggest, furthermore, that it is doubtful that this second section will provide the compensation, the heart balm the minister apparently thinks it is going to provide, especially in respect of the exemption of fruit juices, which consist of at least 95 per cent of pure juice of the fruit, which exemption is to be extended to fruit juices consisting of at least 85 per cent of the pure juice of the fruit.

The Tory government is not satisfied merely to water down its promises but now it is going to water down our fruit juices. However, here we have something which has perhaps a little more appeal if my first glance has not deceived me, and it may be that after all there is something hidden in this amendment which will be a compensation to the people of Canada. Here it is:
That the wording of the exemption for "bases or concentrates for making beverages other than soft drink beverages-
Apparently we cannot have cheaper motor cars but we can make beverages other than soft drinks and can console ourselves in that way, but I must say I find it an odd provision for the present Minister of Finance to be putting into the law.

Bases, not including fruit or imitation fruit bases, for making non-alcoholic-

-fruit bases or fruit concentrates for making beverages, when sold in containers not exceeding ten ounces and consisting of at least 85 per cent of the pure juice of the fruit.
I do not know whether it should be pure fruit juice or pure juices of the fruit. No doubt that is a distinction, as the hon. member for Kootenay West would say, without a difference.
Next we come to paragraph 4, which seems to me will hardly compensate the present aspirants to motor vehicle ownership for not having the tax taken off which the Minister of Finance promised when he was on this side of the house. When such people read that instead of this tax reduction which they expected what they are going to have is an exemption on flavouring extracts-as a matter of fact there seems to be a lot of flavouring in this resolution-in foodstuffs under schedule III, which is to be changed to read:
Food flavouring extracts, emulsions and powders, not including those for beverages.
I think he is likely to be slightly disappointed. The popular appeal of that particular tax reduction will be obvious, and I use the favourite word of the Minister of Finance, to all who read, but I must say I do not know myself what it means.
That is understandable.

Then we come to another section which I admit is a concession of a very sensible nature. This is that desks and chairs designed for classroom use do not have to have a particular design. I realize I have taken a certain amount of the committee's time but I think perhaps if I had been allowed to express myself in the way I originally wished to do I could have said what I had to say much more briefly. Since I am forced to be strictly relevant to the motion before the committee, however, it does somewhat delay my progress. I must say the puritanical note in this particular section does rather astonish me.
Upholstery!
Whether the Minister of Finance has himself always had a hard seat I do not know but why children should be denied upholstery if the school boards want to provide it for them I cannot understand.
Or the whole school, for that matter.

The next paragraph, I think, must have been very close to the minister's heart because it seems to deal with

refractory materials, and I could well understand why the minister would want to remove the tax on refractory materials because there are no materials which the minister handles better than those and in my experience there is nothing much more refractory than the most conciliatory of the minister's speeches, and those which are less conciliatory are even harder. Then we come to materials consumed or expended directly in the process of manufacture or production of goods which are to be clarified and brought into line with the exemption for fuel for lighting or heating, which excludes fuel for use in internal combustion engines. I have no doubt the minister will explain that it is a good thing-

-since he will not take the tax off motor cars, to make sure that he keeps it on the fuel that is used in the motor vehicles. Apparently that is the only object of this section of the resolution if it has any meaning at all.

Advertising sheets, local bulletins, local circulars and similar publications are to be excluded from the exemption for newspapers unless they have qualified as newspapers enjoying second-class mailing privileges. Again, it seems to me that this may have a useful and limited purpose, but that is very far indeed from what we were led to expect would be done in the first budget brought down by the Minister of Finance after all the promises we have heard in two succeeding elections. It seems to me that the rest of the provisions of this section have no real meaning at all so far as the general public is concerned.

Mr. Chairman, there are a number of items that directly affect the building of new housing and the repair of old housing. As I look down the list I see reference to chimneys for buildings. If I were building a house today I should be very glad to note the removal of sales tax on chimneys. There is also provision for the removal of sales tax on assembled or unassembled cabinets, counters, cupboards, furniture, ironing boards, work benches and similar installations. These represent a big reduction in the cost of these articles that 
go into the building of a home and this will also benefit the young and old homebuilder alike.
In the next section there is reference to ash handling and fuel handling equipment for use with furnaces for the heating of buildings when connected directly to such furnaces and installed in the same building as such furnaces. Even the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will realize that the person installing a furnace in a building will receive a considerable saving in respect of the sales tax.
How much?

If a home builder instals an oil burner as most people do today he will require a fuel tank and because fuel tanks are referred to here he will benefit through the removal of the sales tax on this item. When you build a house-despite what has been said by hon. gentlemen in the opposition during the course of this debate- you have to instal a door with a lock and hinges. Here, too, the homebuilder will have a saving in the sales tax on these items. Reference is also made to hard surface plastic laminated building materials and the sales tax has been removed on these items. There is not an hon. member in this house tonight who does not know that those who are building homes today are using more plastic and laminated materials than were ever used in years gone by. The use of these modern building materials is increasing and I commend the minister for removing the sales tax on these items.
I want to assure the minister, those on the treasury benches and hon. members of the house as well that in a constituency such as mine where many of the people are engaged in the building trade and many are improving the existing housing the people there appreciate the savings they will make in respect of these items.

This will have a tremendous impact on the over-all building trades in this country. It will bring about a saving to almost every person engaged in the building of houses who uses these particular materials.
Something was said about advertising. I thought for a minute that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate would seize on the second-class mailing privileges. We did not hear him say anything about that. All I want to say is that the action of the government will promote the distribution of this material without sales tax. Clause 11 reads:
That the annual fee for sales and excise tax licences be abolished.
I understand that the fee was $2 and that it was paid by those who collected the excise taxes for the government. That was the way it used to be under a Liberal administration. Under the present administration the people who collect the tax will not have to take out a licence to collect it. I do not think I need to say anything more about that. There might be some item that we would like to see included.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, the resolution does not relate to the revenue of municipalities but it does relate to the removal of the excise tax on municipal purchases. In the list there is structural aluminum for bridges. I wonder whether the minister is aware that bridges constructed in municipalities are constructed with steel. Steel is largely used for the construction of bridges. I think there is an important omission there. I should like to have the minister's opinion and ask him whether he will not change his mind to include steel for the construction of bridges.
I also wish to express regret in the same way as has been done by my colleague that there is no provision in the resolution to abolish the excise tax on motor vehicles used by municipalities. It has been pointed out that municipalities use trucks in different departments performing various works and also motor cars for police departments. These are important purchases. The provision in the resolution takes care of a few items and the changes are welcome indeed. They are a help but they do not go far enough. I sincerely hope that the Minister of Finance will consider this matter and will bring in an amendment to include the purchase of such things as trucks and automobiles for police departments. These are important purchases involving the spending of a lot of money by municipalities.
There are other items purchased by municipalities which I think should be included in the resolution but which are entirely overlooked. Culverts are included as well as goods for use as part of sewage and drainage systems but I do not see anything here to cover the piping used by waterworks departments. There are other very important omissions that should be considered and I hope
